newsitem.title: USA: U.S. Senate leader seeks chemical treaty documents.
newsitem.headline: U.S. Senate leader seeks chemical treaty documents.

text.p: Senate Majority Leader Trent Lott on Friday urged President Bill Clinton to declassify information and documents related to a global chemical weapons ban before the Senate considers ratifying the accord on Sept.12.
"I regret to inform you that your administration has not been fully cooperative in Senate efforts to obtain critical information," Lott wrote Clinton in a letter.
The Senate agreed in June to vote by Sept. 14 on ratification of the Chemical Weapons Convention, which bans production, stockpiling and use of chemical weapons.

Lott said the Senate's agreement to bring up the treaty was "based on our understanding that the administration could and would be fully forthcoming in the provision of information and documents to enable the Senate to fulfil its constitutional responsibilities."

Signed in January 1993, the chemical weapons treaty has not yet come into force because only 60 of a required 65 countries have so far ratified it. Among those yet to do so are the United States and Russia, the world's two leading chemical weapons powers.
Senate opponents of the treaty have taken issue with provisions that would subject private firms to inspections by an international authority.

Lott is specifically seeking the declassification of critical documents and intelligence community judgments, which are "distinctly different than some public statements made by officials of your administration concerning the convention."

He asked Clinton to reconsider by Tuesday his refusal to declassify certain documents, including a May 21 cable written by Arms Control and Disarmament Agency Director John Holum on Russia's position on the 1990 U.S.-Russian Bilateral Destruction Agreement on chemical weapons.
White House spokesman Barry Toiv said the administration was reviewing the letter.
Another document the Senate is seeking is a July 8 letter from Russian Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin to Vice President Al Gore, Lott said.
